title: Solving State Equations
description: Eigenvalues as poles, modes, the matrix exponential and changes of state coordinates.

study.title: Eigenvalues are the poles
study.body: The denominator of $G(s) = \mathbf{C}(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B} + D$ is $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})$, so the poles are the **eigenvalues** of $\mathbf{A}$ (unless a pole cancels against a zero). For a 2×2 matrix the characteristic equation is $\lambda^2 - \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A})\lambda + \det\mathbf{A} = 0$. The system is asymptotically stable when every eigenvalue has a negative real part; for 2×2 that is exactly $\mathrm{tr}\,\mathbf{A} < 0$ and $\det\mathbf{A} > 0$.

study.title: Modes
study.body: Each eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ has an eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_i$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i$. With distinct eigenvalues the free response is a sum of **modes**; the weights $c_i$ follow from $\mathbf{x}(0) = c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2$. A start on an eigenvector excites only that mode. **Example:** $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$ ($\lambda = -1, -2$) from $\mathbf{x}(0) = [1 \;\; 0]^T$ gives $x_1(t) = 2e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$: the slow mode dominates after a while.

study.title: Complex eigenvalues
study.body: A real matrix has complex eigenvalues in conjugate pairs $\lambda = \sigma \pm j\omega$. Their modes combine into the real functions $e^{\sigma t}\cos\omega t$ and $e^{\sigma t}\sin\omega t$: an oscillation at $\omega$ inside the envelope $e^{\sigma t}$. Negative $\sigma$: decaying, $\sigma = 0$: constant amplitude, positive $\sigma$: growing. The 2 % settling time is about $4/|\sigma|$.

study.title: Explore: eigenvalues and the free response
study.body: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -a_0 & -a_1 \end{bmatrix}$ starts at $\mathbf{x}(0) = [1 \;\; 0]^T$ with no input. With $a_1 = 0$ the eigenvalues sit on the imaginary axis and $x_1$ oscillates forever. Raising $a_1$ moves them left; once $a_1^2 \ge 4a_0$ they become real and the oscillation disappears. A larger $a_0$ raises the oscillation frequency; while the eigenvalues are complex, their real part $-a_1/2$, and so the decay, stays the same.

study.title: The matrix exponential
study.body: The scalar solution $x(t) = e^{at}x(0)$ generalizes with the **matrix exponential** $e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}t + \frac{(\mathbf{A}t)^2}{2!} + \ldots$, also called the state-transition matrix $\Phi(t)$. It is the inverse Laplace transform of $(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}$. An input adds a convolution term. Properties: $e^{\mathbf{0}} = \mathbf{I}$, $e^{\mathbf{A}(t_1 + t_2)} = e^{\mathbf{A}t_1}e^{\mathbf{A}t_2}$, $\frac{d}{dt}e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathbf{A}e^{\mathbf{A}t}$.

study.title: Easy cases
study.body:
- Diagonal: $e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{\lambda_1t}, e^{\lambda_2t})$; the states evolve independently.
- Triangular $\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & b \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \end{bmatrix}$: diagonal entries $e^{\lambda_1t}$, $e^{\lambda_2t}$, top-right $b\frac{e^{\lambda_1t} - e^{\lambda_2t}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$.
- Repeated eigenvalue $\begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}$: a factor $t$ appears (formula below).
- Rotation $\begin{bmatrix} \sigma & \omega \\ -\omega & \sigma \end{bmatrix}$: $e^{\sigma t}\begin{bmatrix} \cos\omega t & \sin\omega t \\ -\sin\omega t & \cos\omega t \end{bmatrix}$.

study.title: Any 2×2 with distinct eigenvalues
study.body:
Write $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ as a sum of the two modes, each with a constant matrix: $\mathbf{M}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \lambda_2\mathbf{I}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ and $\mathbf{M}_2 = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \lambda_1\mathbf{I}}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}$. At $t = 0$ they add up to $\mathbf{I}$.
**Example:** $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$, $\lambda = -1, -2$: $\mathbf{M}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{M}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, so the top-left entry is $2e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$.

study.title: Similarity transforms
study.body: New states $\mathbf{z}$ with $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{T}\mathbf{z}$ give $\dot{\mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}\mathbf{z} + \mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{B}u$ and $y = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{T}\mathbf{z} + Du$. The eigenvalues, trace, determinant and transfer function do not change. With the eigenvectors as columns of $\mathbf{T}$ the new matrix is diagonal (**modal form**): for a companion matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -a_0 & -a_1 \end{bmatrix}$ that is $\mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \lambda_1 & \lambda_2 \end{bmatrix}$.

steps.title: Poles are eigenvalues
steps.body: Without input, $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$. Try $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$: it works when $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, so the natural exponents of the system are the **eigenvalues** of $\mathbf{A}$, the roots of $\det(\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = 0$. They are the poles of every transfer function of the system. For 2×2:

steps.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{bmatrix}$.

ask.prompt: Give the eigenvalue closest to the origin (the slow one).
Give the eigenvalue farthest from the origin (the fast one).
ask.explanation: $\mathrm{tr}\,\mathbf{A}$ = {{l1+l2}}, $\det\mathbf{A}$ = {{l1*l2}}, so $\lambda^2 + {{-(l1+l2)}}\lambda + {{l1*l2}} = 0$ with roots {{l1}} and {{l2}}. The fast one is {{l2}}: its mode $e^{ {{l2}}t}$ dies out first.

steps.prompt: Which $\mathbf{A}$ gives an **asymptotically stable** system $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$?
steps.explanation:
For 2×2, both eigenvalues are in the left half-plane exactly when $\mathrm{tr}\,\mathbf{A} < 0$ **and** $\det\mathbf{A} > 0$ (all coefficients of $\lambda^2 - \mathrm{tr}\,\lambda + \det$ positive).
- $\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$: tr −3, det 3. Stable.
- $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$: tr −3 but det −4: one positive real eigenvalue, despite the negative diagonal.
- $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$: tr +1: growing oscillation.
- $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$: tr 0: eigenvalues $\pm 2j$, oscillates forever (not asymptotically stable).

steps.title: Modes and eigenvectors
steps.body: With distinct eigenvalues the free response is a sum of **modes** $e^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i$. The eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the direction in state space in which that mode moves; it follows from $(\mathbf{A} - \lambda_i\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}$. Only the direction matters, so scale it, for example to first entry 1.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues {{l1}} and {{l2}}. Scale each eigenvector as $\mathbf{v} = [1 \;\; v_2]^T$.

ask.explanation: First row of $(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$: $(a_{11} - \lambda)\cdot 1 + a_{12}v_2 = 0$, so $v_2 = \frac{\lambda - a_{11}}{a_{12}}$ = ({{l1}} − ({{a}}))/({{b}}) = {{p}}. Check with row 2: ({{c}}) + ({{d}} − ({{l1}}))·({{p}}) = 0.
First row of $(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$: $(a_{11} - \lambda) + a_{12}v_2 = 0$, so $v_2 = \frac{\lambda - a_{11}}{a_{12}}$ = ({{l2}} − ({{a}}))/({{b}}) = {{q}}.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalues $-0.25 \pm 2j$. Which graph can be $x_1(t)$ for a nonzero initial state and no input?
steps.explanation: $\lambda = \sigma \pm j\omega$ with $\sigma = -0.25$ and $\omega = 2$: a decaying oscillation $e^{-0.25t}\cos(2t + \phi)$ with period $2\pi/2 \approx 3.1$. The growing oscillation needs $\sigma > 0$, the constant one $\sigma = 0$, and the response without oscillation needs real eigenvalues.

steps.title: Complex eigenvalues
steps.body: A conjugate pair $\lambda = \sigma \pm j\omega$ gives an oscillation at $\omega$ (rad/s) inside the envelope $e^{\sigma t}$. For the companion matrix below the pair is $-\frac{a_1}{2} \pm j\sqrt{a_0 - \frac{a_1^2}{4}}$ when $a_1^2 < 4a_0$. The envelope has dropped to 2 % after about $4/|\sigma|$.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -{{a0}} & -{{a1}} \end{bmatrix}$ has complex eigenvalues $\sigma \pm j\omega$.

ask.prompt: After how long has the envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ dropped to about 2 %?
ask.explanation: $\sigma = -a_1/2$ = −{{a1/2}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (half the trace). The envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ reaches $e^{-4} \approx$ 2 % at $t = 4/|\sigma|$ = {{8/a1|s}}. The imaginary part does not affect the decay.

steps.prompt: Match the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ to the free response.
pairs: Settles to a constant, not always zero
steps.explanation: Real negative eigenvalues give decaying exponentials; complex ones oscillate at their imaginary part with envelope $e^{\sigma t}$. A purely imaginary pair never decays. Any eigenvalue with positive real part makes the response grow. An eigenvalue at 0 gives a constant mode: the state stops but need not return to zero.

steps.title: The state-transition matrix
steps.body: For $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ the solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{x}(0)$, just like $e^{at}x(0)$ for a scalar. The matrix exponential is defined by the same power series, and column $k$ of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ is the response to a unit initial value in state $k$. For a triangular $\mathbf{A}$ you can also solve the equations one by one, starting from the bottom.

steps.prompt: $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} {{l1}} & {{b}} \\ 0 & {{l2}} \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} {{p}} \\ {{q}} \end{bmatrix}$. Find $x_1$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation:
Bottom row first: $\dot x_2 = {{l2}}x_2$, so $x_2(t) = {{q}}e^{ {{l2}}t}$. Then $\dot x_1 = {{l1}}x_1 + {{b}}x_2$, whose solution is the top row of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{x}(0)$:
$$x_1(t) = x_1(0)e^{\lambda_1t} + a_{12}x_2(0)\frac{e^{\lambda_1t} - e^{\lambda_2t}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$$
At $t$ = {{t|s}}: {{p}}·{{exp(l1*t)}} + {{b*q}}·({{exp(l1*t)}} − {{exp(l2*t)}})/({{l1-l2}}) = {{p*exp(l1*t) + q*b*(exp(l1*t) - exp(l2*t))/(l1 - l2)}}.

steps.title: Repeated eigenvalue
steps.body: When both eigenvalues are equal and $\mathbf{A}$ is not diagonal, the modes $e^{\lambda t}$ and $te^{\lambda t}$ appear, just like a double pole in a transfer function. For the standard case $\begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}$: $x_2 = x_2(0)e^{\lambda t}$ drives $x_1$ at its own rate, which produces the factor $t$.

steps.prompt: $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} {{lam}} & 1 \\ 0 & {{lam}} \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} {{p}} \\ {{q}} \end{bmatrix}$. Find $x_1$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $e^{\mathbf{A}t} = e^{\lambda t}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, so $x_1(t) = e^{\lambda t}(x_1(0) + t\,x_2(0))$ = $e^{ {{lam*t}} }$({{p}} + {{t}}·{{q}}) = {{exp(lam*t)}} × {{p+q*t}} = {{exp(lam*t)*(p + q*t)}}.

steps.title: Any 2×2 with distinct eigenvalues
steps.body: Split $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ into its two modes: $e^{\mathbf{A}t} = e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf{M}_1 + e^{\lambda_2t}\mathbf{M}_2$ with $\mathbf{M}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \lambda_2\mathbf{I}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ and $\mathbf{M}_2 = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \lambda_1\mathbf{I}}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}$. Each entry is a fixed combination of $e^{\lambda_1t}$ and $e^{\lambda_2t}$. The same result follows from partial fractions of $(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}$.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ {{-l1*l2}} & {{l1+l2}} \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues {{l1}} and {{l2}}.

ask.prompt: Find the top-right entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
ask.explanation: Top-right entries: $\mathbf{M}_1$ has $\frac{a_{12}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2} = \frac{1}{ {{l1-l2}} }$, $\mathbf{M}_2$ has $\frac{1}{ {{l2-l1}} }$. So the entry is $\frac{e^{\lambda_1t} - e^{\lambda_2t}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ = ({{exp(l1*t)}} − {{exp(l2*t)}})/{{l1-l2}} = {{(exp(l1*t) - exp(l2*t))/(l1 - l2)}}.

ask.prompt: Find the top-left entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
ask.explanation: Top-left entries: $\mathbf{M}_1$: $\frac{0 - \lambda_2}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ = {{-l2/(l1-l2)}}, $\mathbf{M}_2$: $\frac{0 - \lambda_1}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}$ = {{-l1/(l2-l1)}}. Entry = {{-l2/(l1-l2)}}·{{exp(l1*t)}} + ({{-l1/(l2-l1)}})·{{exp(l2*t)}} = {{(l1*exp(l2*t) - l2*exp(l1*t))/(l1 - l2)}}. (Check: at $t = 0$ it is 1.)

steps.prompt: For any two square matrices, $e^{(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{F})t} = e^{\mathbf{A}t}e^{\mathbf{F}t}$.
steps.explanation: That rule holds for numbers because $ab = ba$. Matrices generally do not commute: multiply out the series and the cross terms only match when $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{A}$. What does always hold is $e^{\mathbf{A}(t_1 + t_2)} = e^{\mathbf{A}t_1}e^{\mathbf{A}t_2}$, because $\mathbf{A}$ commutes with itself.

steps.prompt: $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} {{l1}} & 0 \\ 0 & {{l2}} \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x} + \begin{bmatrix} {{b1}} \\ {{b2}} \end{bmatrix}u$ starts at $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{0}$; at $t = 0$ a step $u$ = {{u0}} is applied. Find $x_2$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: The states are decoupled. $x_2(t) = \int_0^t e^{\lambda_2(t-\tau)}b_2u_0\,d\tau = \frac{b_2u_0}{-\lambda_2}\left(1 - e^{\lambda_2t}\right)$ = ({{b2}}·{{u0}}/{{-l2}})(1 − {{exp(l2*t)}}) = {{b2*u0/(-l2)*(1 - exp(l2*t))}}. It rises like a first-order step response toward $b_2u_0/|\lambda_2|$ = {{b2*u0/(-l2)}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ with the Laplace transform in order.
items: Split every entry into partial fractions
Take the inverse Laplace transform of every entry
steps.explanation: $\mathcal{L}\{e^{\mathbf{A}t}\} = (s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}$. Each entry is a rational function with the eigenvalues as poles; partial fractions turn it into terms $\frac{r}{s - \lambda_i}$, which transform back to $re^{\lambda_it}$.

steps.prompt: A mass-spring-damper has $m$ = {{m}} kg, $k$ = {{k}} N/m and $b$ = {{b}} N·s/m, so $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -k/m & -b/m \end{bmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $\sigma \pm j\omega$.

ask.explanation: $\det(\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = \lambda^2 + \frac{b}{m}\lambda + \frac{k}{m} = \lambda^2 + {{b/m}}\lambda + {{k/m}}$. The real part of a complex pair is half the trace: $\sigma = -\frac{b}{2m}$ = {{-b/(2*m)}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

$\lambda^2 + {{b/m}}\lambda + {{k/m}} = 0$: $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m} - \sigma^2} = \sqrt{ {{k/m}} - {{(b/(2*m))^2}} }$ = {{sqrt(k/m - (b/(2*m))^2)}} rad/s, slightly below the undamped $\sqrt{k/m}$ = {{sqrt(k/m)}} rad/s.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the free response $x(t) = x(0)e^{\lambda t}$ of a first-order mode. Read the graph and find the eigenvalue $\lambda$.
steps.explanation: After one time constant $\tau = 1/|\lambda|$ the response has dropped to $e^{-1}$ = 36.8 % of its start: {{0.368*x0}}. The curve passes that level at $t \approx$ {{tau|s}}, so $\lambda = -1/\tau$ = {{-1/tau}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ {{-l1*l2}} & {{l1+l2}} \end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues {{l1}}, {{l2}}), $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [{{c0}} \;\; {{c1}}]$. Transform to modal form with $\mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ {{l1}} & {{l2}} \end{bmatrix}$.

ask.explanation: $\det\mathbf{T} = \lambda_2 - \lambda_1$ = {{l2-l1}}, so $\mathbf{T}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ {{l2-l1}} }\begin{bmatrix} {{l2}} & -1 \\ {{-l1}} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Its last column is $\bar{\mathbf{B}}$: first entry $-1/({{l2-l1}})$ = {{1/(l1-l2)}}.

$\mathbf{C}\mathbf{T} = [c_0 + c_1\lambda_1 \;\; c_0 + c_1\lambda_2]$: first entry {{c0}} + {{c1}}·({{l1}}) = {{c0 + c1*l1}}. In modal form the transfer function is $\frac{\bar c_1\bar b_1}{s - \lambda_1} + \frac{\bar c_2\bar b_2}{s - \lambda_2}$: its partial fractions.

steps.prompt: A similarity transformation $\bar{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}$ changes the eigenvectors but not the eigenvalues.
steps.explanation: $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}) = \det\big(\mathbf{T}^{-1}(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{T}\big)$ $= \det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})$: same characteristic polynomial. An eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ becomes $\mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}$, the same physical mode described in the new coordinates.

steps.prompt: $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} {{sg}} & {{w}} \\ {{-w}} & {{sg}} \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x}(0) = [1 \;\; 0]^T$. Find $x_1$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: This is the rotation form with eigenvalues $\sigma \pm j\omega$ = {{sg}} ± j{{w}}: $e^{\mathbf{A}t} = e^{\sigma t}\begin{bmatrix} \cos\omega t & \sin\omega t \\ -\sin\omega t & \cos\omega t \end{bmatrix}$. So $x_1 = e^{\sigma t}\cos\omega t$ = $e^{ {{sg*t}} }\cos({{w*t}})$ = {{exp(sg*t)}} × {{cos(w*t)}} = {{exp(sg*t)*cos(w*t)}} (angle in radians).

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -{{a0}} & -a_1 \end{bmatrix}$. Set $a_1$ so that the free response settles (2 %) in about $T_s$ = {{Ts|s}}.
steps.explanation: For a complex pair $\lambda = -\frac{a_1}{2} \pm j\sqrt{a_0 - \frac{a_1^2}{4}}$, so the decay rate is $|\sigma| = a_1/2$. $T_s \approx 4/|\sigma|$ gives $|\sigma| = 4/T_s$ = {{4/Ts}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $a_1 = 2|\sigma|$ = {{8/Ts}}. The eigenvalues then sit on the orange line Re(s) = −{{4/Ts}}; $a_0$ only moves them up and down.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ {{-l1*l2}} & {{l1+l2}} \end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues {{l1}} and {{l2}}) starts at $\mathbf{x}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} {{p}} \\ {{qq}} \end{bmatrix}$ with no input. Find $x_1$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.answer: p*(l1*exp(l2*t) - l2*exp(l1*t))/(l1 - l2) + qq*(exp(l1*t) - exp(l2*t))/(l1 - l2)
steps.explanation:
Row 1 of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ from $\mathbf{M}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \lambda_2\mathbf{I}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ and $\mathbf{M}_2 = \frac{\mathbf{A} - \lambda_1\mathbf{I}}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}$:
$\Phi_{11} = \frac{\lambda_1e^{\lambda_2t} - \lambda_2e^{\lambda_1t}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ = {{(l1*exp(l2*t) - l2*exp(l1*t))/(l1 - l2)}}, $\Phi_{12} = \frac{e^{\lambda_1t} - e^{\lambda_2t}}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}$ = {{(exp(l1*t) - exp(l2*t))/(l1 - l2)}}.
$x_1 = \Phi_{11}x_1(0) + \Phi_{12}x_2(0)$ = {{(l1*exp(l2*t) - l2*exp(l1*t))/(l1 - l2)}}·{{p}} + {{(exp(l1*t) - exp(l2*t))/(l1 - l2)}}·({{qq}}) = {{p*(l1*exp(l2*t) - l2*exp(l1*t))/(l1 - l2) + qq*(exp(l1*t) - exp(l2*t))/(l1 - l2)}}.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ {{-l1*l2}} & {{l1+l2}} \end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues {{l1}}, {{l2}}), $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{0}$, unit step input.

ask.explanation:
$X_1(s) = \frac{1}{s(s - \lambda_1)(s - \lambda_2)}$ (companion form: $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$ gives $\frac{1}{s^2 + a_1s + a_0}$). Partial fractions:
$$x_1(t) = \frac{1}{\lambda_1\lambda_2} + \frac{e^{\lambda_1t}}{\lambda_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)} + \frac{e^{\lambda_2t}}{\lambda_2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)}$$
= {{1/(l1*l2)}} + ({{exp(l1*t)/(l1*(l1 - l2))}}) + ({{exp(l2*t)/(l2*(l2 - l1))}}) = {{1/(l1*l2) + exp(l1*t)/(l1*(l1 - l2)) + exp(l2*t)/(l2*(l2 - l1))}}.

In steady state $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{0}$: $\mathbf{x}_{ss} = -\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B}$. Row 2 gives $-{{l1*l2}}x_1 + 0 + 1 = 0$, so $x_1 = 1/(\lambda_1\lambda_2)$ = 1/{{l1*l2}} = {{1/(l1*l2)}}.

steps.prompt: $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} {{sg}} & {{w}} \\ {{-w}} & {{sg}} \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} {{p}} \\ {{qq}} \end{bmatrix}$. Find $x_2$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $e^{\mathbf{A}t} = e^{\sigma t}\begin{bmatrix} \cos\omega t & \sin\omega t \\ -\sin\omega t & \cos\omega t \end{bmatrix}$ with $\sigma$ = {{sg}}, $\omega$ = {{w}}. Row 2: $x_2 = e^{\sigma t}(-x_1(0)\sin\omega t + x_2(0)\cos\omega t)$ = {{exp(sg*t)}} × (−{{p}}·{{sin(w*t)}} + {{qq}}·{{cos(w*t)}}) = {{exp(sg*t)*(-p*sin(w*t) + qq*cos(w*t))}}.

steps.prompt: Which matrix can **not** be a state-transition matrix $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ for any constant $\mathbf{A}$?
steps.explanation: Every $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ equals $\mathbf{I}$ at $t = 0$ (no time, no change). $\mathrm{diag}(e^{-t}, 2e^{-2t})$ gives $\mathrm{diag}(1, 2)$ at $t = 0$, so it is impossible. The others are $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ for $\mathbf{A} = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -3)$, for the rotation $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, and for the double integrator $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues {{l1}} and {{l2}}. The system starts at $\mathbf{x}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} {{k}} \\ {{k*p}} \end{bmatrix}$ with no input. Find $x_1$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: Check whether $\mathbf{x}(0)$ is an eigenvector: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}(0) = [{{a*k + b*k*p}} \;\; {{c*k + d*k*p}}]^T$, which is {{l1}} times $\mathbf{x}(0)$. It is, for $\lambda$ = {{l1}}, so only that mode is excited and the state slides along the eigenvector: $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{x}(0)$. $x_1$ = {{k}}$e^{ {{l1*t}} }$ = {{k*exp(l1*t)}}.

steps.prompt: The graph shows $x_1(t)$ of a system with complex eigenvalues $\sigma \pm j\omega$ after an initial displacement. Read the period and find $\omega$.
steps.explanation: Successive peaks are one period $T_d$ = {{2*pi/w|s}} apart. $\omega = 2\pi/T_d$ = {{w}} rad/s. (The envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ only sets how fast the peaks shrink.)

steps.prompt: If every eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$ has a negative real part, every entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ tends to 0 as $t \to \infty$.
steps.explanation: Every entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}t}$ is a combination of the modes $e^{\lambda_it}$ (times powers of $t$ for repeated eigenvalues). With $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i < 0$ each of them decays, even $te^{\lambda t}$, so $e^{\mathbf{A}t} \to \mathbf{0}$ and every free response returns to the origin: asymptotic stability.
